findings.summary: The booking tangent series is not visible as its own series. It is drawn before the assembly series and at the same zorder (scripts/prototypes/bank_step_batch/plot.py:40-45, where every stage is plotted with zorder=3 in tuple order), so the mauve assembly line and its markers cover it wherever the two coincide. They coincide almost everywhere: 108.97 ms against 110.55 ms at 64 slices, under one pixel apart on this three-decade axis. Measured on the render, the mauve series has 4,012 core pixels in the band where the pair runs against 660 for the red one, and in the marker columns for 4, 16 and 64 slices the red series has 0, 1 and 1 core pixels against 8-11 mauve pixels each, so all three booking-tangent markers are hidden behind the assembly markers. The legend still promises a red 'booking tangent' series and a reader comparing the swatch with the plotted band cannot tell which of the two lines is which, or verify that the booking-tangent value at 64 slices is 109 ms rather than the assembly 111 ms. The stage breakdown is the figure's whole purpose, so a reader is stopped on one of its five stage series. A second cue (a dash pattern, a marker shape, or a lightness step) would separate them without moving the data.

The booking tangent is drawn in #e45756, a red, for an ordinary stage series. The repository's plotting rules keep red for a limit being broken (AGENTS.md, 'Spend colour on the subject'), and this figure has no limit and no failure: the series is the largest per-slice stage cost that batching does not reduce. On the page the red reads as an alarm or a breached threshold, which is the opposite of what the series means, and it is also the colour most easily confused with the neighbouring mauve assembly line at this size.

The whole-step series stops at 16 slices because its 64-slice measurement never landed (the measurement job segfaulted, per the caption), and nothing in the figure marks that as a truncation rather than an end point. A missing stage row becomes np.nan at plot.py:41 and simply drops the point, so the near-black series ends mid-frame with an ordinary marker. A reader who does not read the caption can take the absence of a 64-slice whole-step point as an oversight, or mistake the flatter 131 ms end point for the stage having converged. The caption does state the segfault, so this is a figure-only gap, not a wrong picture.

The caption says 'The whole step and the read fall with batch size', but no series in the figure is named 'the read': the falling series beside the whole step is labelled 'residual and booking'. A reader who follows the caption to the legend finds no 'read' entry and has to infer that the read's per-slice cost is the residual-and-booking series. Naming the series the caption means would remove the inference.

rubric_lines: RUBRIC per-slice-wall.svg legibility: fail. Five of the six series read at a glance on the log-log axes, but the booking tangent (red #e45756) is drawn beneath the assembly series (mauve #b279a2) and the two lie about 1.5 ms apart on a three-decade axis, so the red series renders as a thin fringe and its markers at 4, 16 and 64 slices are covered by the mauve markers; one of the five stage series cannot be read as its own series. Finding 1.

RUBRIC per-slice-wall.svg table_form: pass. Per-slice wall against slices per batch is a genuine plotted relationship, not a table in disguise: the fall in per-slice cost with batch size and the flatness of two of the stages are shape facts the 24 underlying numbers do not carry on their own.
